works.title: The Starry Night
works.one_line: the night sky as weather of the soul — painted by day, from a barred room
works.location_now: Museum of Modern Art, New York

feeling.text: Stand before it and the sky will not hold still. Eleven stars and a fat lemon moon pulse inside their own haloes while the blue between them rolls up into scrolls — you feel wind before you can name it. Below, a village sleeps, small and warm-windowed; a cypress rears between you and all that motion like a dark flame. It is agitation and comfort at once: the night is enormous, and the night is watching over the houses. Strangest of all, the agitation is real physics. In 2006 researchers showed that the flicker of light across his most troubled-period paintings matches the statistics of turbulent flow, and in 2024 a study of the fourteen swirls found Kolmogorov's law of turbulence — written half a century after his death — hiding in the brushwork. The picture does not depict turbulence; it performs it.

hands.text: He had been inside Saint-Paul-de-Mausole about six weeks. The ear was six months healed: he had cut into it in Arles on the night of 23 December 1888, and after neighbours petitioned to have him confined, he chose the asylum himself, signing in on 8 May 1889. Theo paid for two small cells with barred windows — one to sleep in, one to paint in. From the bedroom he watched the dawn: 'This morning I saw the countryside from my window a long time before sunrise, with nothing but the morning star, which looked very big.' That star was Venus, truly blazing that spring. He was not allowed to paint upstairs, so around 18 June he built the night by daylight, in the studio below, partly from memory — real Venus, real Alpilles hills, an invented village, a cypress pulled close. To Theo he called it only 'a new study of a starry sky.'

facts.claim: Van Gogh cut off part of his left ear in Arles on the night of 23 December 1888, after a breakdown while living with Gauguin.
In February 1889 his Arles neighbours petitioned to have him institutionalised, and he was confined in the Arles hospital before choosing the asylum.
He voluntarily entered the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole near Saint-Rémy on 8 May 1889; Theo arranged two adjoining cells with barred windows, the second used as a studio.
In letter 777 (c. 31 May–6 June 1889) he described watching the morning star from his window long before sunrise.
On or about 18 June 1889 he told Theo he had painted 'a new study of a starry sky' (letter 782), adding that work 'occupies and distracts me – which I need very much'.

The picture was painted by day in his ground-floor studio around mid-June 1889; the view from his east-facing bedroom window held wheat fields and hills, while the village was invented and the cypress exaggerated and pulled close.
Astronomical research confirms Venus was visible at dawn in Provence in spring 1889, near its maximum brightness.

world.text: France spent 1889 throwing itself a hundredth-birthday party. In Paris the Exposition Universelle opened in May — the centennial fair of the Revolution — and the just-finished Eiffel Tower took in nearly twelve thousand visitors a day; thirty-two million people passed through the fair by autumn. Theo, who paid Vincent's bills from his art-dealer salary, had married Jo Bonger in Amsterdam that April. Seven hundred kilometres south, Provence kept older time: wheat, olives, cicadas, the mistral wind. Saint-Rémy was a small town under the Alpilles, and the asylum — a monastery centuries old, run by Dr Théophile Peyron, once a navy doctor — had rooms to spare, which is how Vincent got a second cell for a studio. While the modern world rode elevators up iron latticework, he walked out with an orderly to paint, and in his year there made roughly 150 paintings.

facts.claim: The Exposition Universelle ran in Paris from 6 May to 31 October 1889 (the Eiffel Tower itself opened to visitors 15 May), marking the centennial of the French Revolution; it drew 32,250,297 visitors, 1,953,122 of them up the tower — almost 12,000 a day.
Theo van Gogh married Johanna (Jo) Bonger in Amsterdam on 17 April 1889, three weeks before Vincent entered the asylum.
The asylum, a former monastery set among wheat fields, vineyards and olive trees, was run by Dr Théophile Peyron, a former naval doctor.
In his year at Saint-Rémy Van Gogh produced about 150 paintings and around 100 drawings.

paint.text: The sky is two blues doing different jobs: synthetic ultramarine — the cheap factory-made successor to ground lapis lazuli — for the deep night, and cobalt blue, pricier and cooler, for the bright swirls and the air around the moon. The moon and stars glow with Indian yellow over zinc yellow; emerald green, an arsenic pigment, threads around the moon; ochre, lead white and Prussian blue do quieter work in the village and the cypress. Scientists from RIT and MoMA mapped every pigment with multispectral imaging. One worry hides in the stars: zinc yellow is a chromate, chemical kin of the chrome yellow that X-ray work in 2011 caught browning in his Sunflowers under light. The stars we see now are likely dimmer than the ones he painted. These were modern industrial colours, some only decades old, ordered from Paris on Theo's money.

pigments.name: Synthetic (artificial) ultramarine
pigments.note: The deep blue night sky around the stars; a cheap industrial version of the lapis lazuli blue that had once cost more than gold.

pigments.name: Cobalt blue
pigments.note: The brighter swirling sky and the area around the moon; an expensive cobalt-aluminate blue invented in 1802.

pigments.name: Indian yellow
pigments.note: The deeper golden glow of moon and stars.

pigments.name: Zinc yellow
pigments.note: In the moon and stars; a zinc-chromate yellow prone to darkening with light — the stars were likely once brighter.

pigments.name: Emerald green
pigments.note: Green strokes around the moon; a copper-arsenic pigment, brilliant and poisonous.

pigments.name: Prussian blue
pigments.note: Likely mixed into the dark green of the cypress.

pigments.name: Yellow ochre and lead white
pigments.note: The quieter earths and pale bodies of strokes through village and sky.

facts.claim: Multispectral imaging by Rochester Institute of Technology and MoMA (Zhao, Berns, Taplin, Coddington) mapped the pigments: ultramarine and cobalt blue in the sky, Indian yellow and zinc yellow in the moon and stars, possibly cadmium yellow in the brightest halos.

X-ray studies published in 2011 showed that chrome yellow (lead chromate) in Van Gogh's paintings darkens under light through photo-reduction of the chromium — the chemistry behind his fading yellows.
The painting is oil on canvas, 73.7 x 92.1 cm.

afterlife.text: He sent it to Theo in Paris that autumn and never sold it. Theo died in January 1891, six months after Vincent, and the canvas passed to Theo's widow, Jo van Gogh-Bonger, who spent her life making the world see her brother-in-law. She sold it in 1900 to the poet Julien Leclercq; it went to the painter Émile Schuffenecker, then back to Jo, then through Rotterdam's Oldenzeel Gallery to Georgette van Stolk, who kept it from 1906 to 1938. The dealer Paul Rosenberg bought it and in 1940 fled Paris ahead of the Nazis. In 1941 the young Museum of Modern Art traded him two Cézannes and a Toulouse-Lautrec for it, paid for by the bequest of Lillie P. Bliss — a founder who died in 1931, never owned a Van Gogh, and wrote a will that let her pictures be sold to catch the next ones. It has hung in New York ever since — and now physicists queue in front of it too.

facts.claim: Provenance: Theo van Gogh; his widow Jo van Gogh-Bonger; sold 1900 to Julien Leclercq; to Émile Schuffenecker 1901; repurchased by Jo; via Oldenzeel Gallery, Rotterdam, to Georgette P. van Stolk (1906–1938); to dealer Paul Rosenberg, who fled Nazi-occupied France to New York in 1940.
MoMA acquired the painting in 1941 from Rosenberg by exchanging two Cézannes and a Toulouse-Lautrec; the credit line reads 'Acquired through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest (by exchange)'.

Lillie P. Bliss, one of MoMA's three female founders, died in 1931 two years after the museum opened; her bequest permitted works to be sold or exchanged to acquire new ones, which funded The Starry Night.
In 2006, Aragón and colleagues showed the luminance fluctuations in Van Gogh's troubled-period paintings, including The Starry Night, match Kolmogorov's statistical theory of turbulence.
A 2024 study in Physics of Fluids analysed the painting's 14 swirls and found the -5/3 Kolmogorov power law of turbulence, plus Batchelor scaling in the brushstrokes.

quotes.text: This morning I saw the countryside from my window a long time before sunrise with nothing but the morning star, which looked very big.
quotes.who: Vincent van Gogh, letter 777 to Theo, Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, c. 31 May–6 June 1889

quotes.text: That doesn't stop me having a tremendous need for, shall I say the word — for religion — so I go outside at night to paint the stars.
quotes.who: Vincent van Gogh, letter 691 to Theo, Arles, c. 29 September 1888

quotes.text: Once again I'm allowing myself to do stars too big, &c., new setback, and I've enough of that.
quotes.who: Vincent van Gogh, letter 822 to Émile Bernard, Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, c. 26 November 1889 — his own late verdict on the picture

works.title: The Fighting Temeraire
works.one_line: a warship towed to dismantling — Turner places oak, wind, steam, and smoke in one invented sunset
works.location_now: National Gallery, London · Room 40 (as of 2026-08-20; gallery locations can change)
works.image_alt: Turner's pale three-masted warship recedes behind a small dark steam tug on the Thames; smoke crosses the ship while a red invented sunset fills the right half of the sky.

revision.scope: The feeling, world, and afterlife prose and the lens-referenced Temeraire facts were revised; three secondary context claims and two secondary afterlife claims no longer used by the prose were removed.
revision.method: The revised claims were re-read against current National Gallery, Royal Museums Greenwich, Southwark Council, and Bank of England records. Independent read-only passes challenged teleology, collective feeling, source custody, missing accounts, rights, and correction language.
revision.limits: This was not a new full audit of every unchanged paint, pigment, quotation, or historical claim in the five strata; those retain the dataset's earlier verification date.

feeling.text: A pale ship rises like a ghost behind a small dark tug. The masts are bare, the tug coughs fire and soot, and long rays from the sunset lean back towards the hull. The composition invites an elegiac reading: wood and rope are made luminous while steam is made compact, black, and urgent. That response belongs to this reading, not every viewer. Turner has staged a farewell, not recorded one exactly; the feeling begins in the choices he made.

hands.text: Turner was sixty-three, rich, famous and solitary, living over his own dusty gallery in Queen Anne Street, where a visitor found brilliant pictures 'shining out of the dirt and neglect'. He almost certainly never saw the tow — he may not even have been in England that September, since he usually spent late summer sketching in Europe. He read about it afterwards: the last great Trafalgar ship but one, sold out of the Navy and dragged to a breaker's yard. He worked fast, with four other large canvases to finish for the 1839 Royal Academy, and painted it over a discarded canvas that already carried a big sail — X-rays still show it under the tug. He hung it with borrowed lines about a flag that no longer flew. Then he would not let it go: not for £5,000, not for a blank cheque. 'My Darling', he called it.

facts.claim: Turner probably learned of the ship's fate from press reports in late September 1838 and 'must have worked fairly swiftly' on the picture for the spring 1839 Royal Academy, where he showed four other paintings of about the same size.

It is unlikely Turner witnessed the tow — he may not even have been in England at the time; he usually travelled in Europe in August and September. Later legends that he saw it from Greenwich, Blackwall Reach, a Margate steamer or a Bermondsey pier are unfounded, and Turner never claimed to be an eye-witness.

Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1839 as 'The Fighting Temeraire, tugged to her last Berth to be broken up, 1838', with lines Turner adapted from Thomas Campbell's 'Ye Mariners of England': 'The flag which braved the battle and the breeze, / No longer owns her.'
In a pencil draft letter of about 1845, refusing another loan of the picture, Turner wrote that 'no consid[eratio]ns of money or favour can induce me to lend my Darling again'.

In 1848 the American collector James Lenox, calling with the dealer Thomas Griffith, reputedly offered £5,000 and then a blank cheque; Turner refused, having by then determined to leave the picture to the nation (recorded by C.R. Leslie).

Lady Trevelyan, visiting Turner's Queen Anne Street gallery around 1844, recalled faded, barely weather-tight walls, furniture thick with dust, and 'the glorious Temeraire lighting up another corner'.

world.text: The Temeraire was a state-owned warship built from more than 5,000 oaks at Chatham and launched in 1798. At Trafalgar in 1805 it fought directly astern of Nelson's Victory. From 1820 it lay off Sheerness, chiefly as a supply ship. In 1838 the Admiralty stripped its reusable equipment and sold the 2,110-ton hull to the Rotherhithe ship-breaker John Beatson for £5,530. Two steam tugs moved it up the Thames on 5–6 September. Turner probably did not see that journey: the real hull was mastless, two tugs worked the tow, and it arrived before sunset. The painting puts sail and steam beside each other, but that composition is not evidence that one age, one public, or one civilisation understood technical change in a single way.

facts.claim: Designed as a 98-gun ship of the line, built of the wood of over 5,000 oaks in the Royal Navy's dockyard at Chatham, and launched there on 11 September 1798.

At Trafalgar (21 October 1805), under Captain Eliab Harvey and stationed immediately astern of the Victory, the Temeraire saved Nelson's flagship from being boarded from the Redoutable by firing a larboard broadside into her, while simultaneously firing her other side into the Fougueux; she took both French ships as prizes.
From 1820 she lay moored off Sheerness, chiefly as a victualling ship, never moving for eighteen years; by 1838, 14 of the 27 ships in Nelson's Trafalgar fleet had already been sold to be broken up.

Sold by Dutch auction on 16 August 1838 at the Navy Board offices in Somerset House to John Beatson, Rotherhithe ship-breaker and timber merchant, for £5,530 — the Navy had first stripped her of masts, yards, guns, anchors and stores, leaving a 2,110-ton empty hull.

The tow took place on 5–6 September 1838, by the steam tugs Samson and London hired from the Thames Steam Towing Company, timed to the spring tides after the 4 September full moon; she was probably secure at Beatson's wharf before 3 pm on 6 September.

Turner's sun sets in the wrong direction — a ship coming up the Thames heads west, so the sunset could not lie astern of her in the east; James Dafforne first pointed out the 'glaring error' in 1877, sparking a lively but inconclusive correspondence in The Times.

He also took deliberate liberties: the mastless hulk is shown with her three lower masts in and partly rigged, her black-and-yellow paintwork turned white and gold, only one tug shown pulling (the second just visible in the distance), and the tug's funnel moved in front of its mast so the smoke streams back through the Temeraire's masts.

paint.text: It is oil on a second-hand canvas: under the tug, X-rays show a large sail Turner had once laid in and abandoned. The sunset is built physically — thick ridges of paint for the sun and clouds, standing proud of the surface, with thin coloured glazes floated over them. Turner famously grabbed new factory-made colours almost as soon as the chemists produced them; the chrome yellows of the industrial age glow through this period of his skies. A popular story says this sky blazed with iodine scarlet, a gorgeous mercury red that dies in daylight, and was already fading by 1859 — yet the Gallery's own examiners call the sunset 'unusually intact', so hold that story loosely. And the Tambora legend fails here on arithmetic: volcanic reddening shows in paintings only for about three years after an eruption, and Tambora blew in 1815. This sunset needed no volcano. It is pure invention — the real tow ended by mid-afternoon.

pigments.name: Lead white
pigments.note: The sun's disc and the ridged clouds are 'applied so thickly in places that the paint stands proud from the canvas' — white-lead impasto doing the work of light itself.

pigments.name: Chrome yellow (lead chromate)
pigments.note: The new industrial yellow of Turner's lifetime; analyses of his late work show him using the fresh synthetic colours — chrome yellow for the bright yellows, cobalt blue, emerald green — as an early adopter.

pigments.name: Iodine scarlet (mercuric iodide)
pigments.note: A brilliant but notoriously fugitive red in Turner's palette. Popular accounts place it in this sky and say the reds were fading by 1859 — but the National Gallery's technical notes call the sunset 'unusually intact', so the claim is unverified.

pigments.name: Megilp (mastic resin and oil gel)
pigments.note: The buttery gelled medium British painters of the period stirred into oil paint to make impasto stand up; documented in Townsend's studies of nineteenth-century British practice, though no public analysis names it in this specific canvas.

facts.claim: Oil on canvas, 90.7 × 121.6 cm.
An X-radiograph shows a large sail, on a much bigger scale, where the tug's mast, rigging and funnel now lie — Turner reused a discarded canvas on which he had laid in a large sailing-boat.

The dramatic sunset effects were 'achieved by the use of impasto and glazes' and are 'unusually intact': the picture has not been cleaned or varnished since arriving with the Turner Bequest in 1856; surface dirt was removed in 1945, and flaking paint forced a lining in 1963. The stretcher is probably original. Full technical examination: Martin Wyld and Ashok Roy, in Egerton 1995.
'Turner did use new pigments soon after they became available' — he is the standing example of an artist adopting the century's new synthetic colours quickly (Joyce Townsend, Tate Papers).

Volcanic-sunset claims mostly fail here: reddened skies show in paintings only for the eruption year plus about three after (Zerefos), and Tambora blew in 1815 — 24 years too early. One narrow door remains: Cosigüina erupted January 1835, and Turner began the picture around October 1838 — only the sky's earliest layers could carry that tint. The blaze is best credited to Turner.

The sunset is Turner's invention on its own terms too: by an expert reckoning from the 1838 tide-tables (van der Merwe and Robson), the Temeraire was secured in her last berth by about 3 pm, several hours before sunset in early September.

afterlife.text: Turner kept the painting until his death in 1851 and intended it for the nation. It entered the National Gallery with the Turner Bequest in 1856. Material from the dismantled ship also continued: Royal Museums Greenwich holds an oak table made from its timber. In 2020 the painting entered another kind of circulation on the Bank of England's polymer £20 note beside Turner's self-portrait. A bequest, a salvaged table, a museum display, and a banknote preserve different things. Their survival and circulation do not establish one national memory, one response, or one measure of thriving.

facts.claim: Turner refused all offers for the picture — reputedly £5,000 and then a blank cheque from James Lenox in 1848 — 'because he intended to leave it to the nation'; he kept it until his death in 1851.
It entered the National Gallery with the Turner Bequest in 1856 and was among the first paintings of the Bequest to be hung; it remains one of the Gallery's most popular paintings.
Royal Museums Greenwich holds an oak table made from the Temeraire's timber after John Beatson broke up the ship in autumn 1838.
The Bank of England put The Fighting Temeraire behind Turner's self-portrait on the polymer £20 note, which entered circulation in February 2020.
The National Gallery's live holding record listed the painting in Room 40 when checked on 20 August 2026; gallery locations can change.

civilisation_lens.question: What can this one painting reveal — and not reveal — about resource use, labour, state power, technical change, dismantling, and public memory in one British context?
civilisation_lens.scope: This one work shows how a specific state warship became scrap and then a national image. It does not represent British civilisation, its workers, its opponents, or everyone affected by naval power.

frame.kingdom_effect: This lens does not register Artbitrage, adopt a foundation, create citizenship, or speak for KINGDOM.

visible_boundaries: One work, many relations, no claim to speak for a people.
This is an Artbitrage reading. Turner's recorded words and museum records are named where used. No living person is represented here as speaking for a group or civilisation.
Missing accounts remain missing. Their absence is not agreement, refusal, or proof that no account exists.
This lens does not decide that sail, steam, Britain, war, industry, or this painting represents a stage of civilisation, progress, sustainability, or thriving.

source_custody.holding_authority_limit: The National Gallery is authoritative for its own holding, catalogue, and conservation record; it does not own every meaning or relation around the work or ship.

left.label: oak · wind · naval system
left.text: A state warship made from long-grown timber, rigging, stored labour, and organised violence.

juxtaposition.centre: The 1838 tow: a stripped hull, two hired steam tugs, a tide, and a private breaker's yard.

right.label: steam · company · river industry
right.text: A hired steam-towing service in the Thames river economy, powered by a different material and commercial system.

juxtaposition.boundary: These are two material systems in relation, not a before-and-after ladder. Sail is not sustainable innocence; steam is not progress by itself.

evidence.claim: William Beatson's September 1838 drawing records the Temeraire as a mastless hull at John Beatson's Rotherhithe wharf.
evidence.attribution_basis: institutional object record for a contemporary drawing
evidence.limits: The record describes one drawing and its inscription; it is not testimony from the towing or breaking workers.

evidence.claim: Royal Museums Greenwich identifies the Thames Steam Towing Company tugs London and Samson as the two vessels paid to tow the Temeraire on 5–6 September 1838.
evidence.attribution_basis: institutional manuscript record referring to Beatson's ledger
evidence.limits: The record names the company and tugs, not the workers or their conditions.

evidence.claim: Southwark Council names shipbuilding and ship-breaking in Rotherhithe among the borough's important industrial archaeology.
evidence.limits: This establishes local industrial context, not a worker account or the effect of this one dismantling.

evidence.claim: The National Gallery's visitor policy says access to the permanent collection is free, subject to stated capacity, security, and access conditions.
evidence.limits: Free general admission does not establish that every person can reach, use, or understand the collection.

facets.title: origin, language, authority
facets.question: Whose name and account open the record?

reading.text: The English exhibition title turns one decommissioned warship into an elegy. That is a documented framing, not an authorised account of a people or of everyone drawn into the ship's history.

unknowns: No authorised French- or Spanish-language account is attached.
No source owner has authorised Artbitrage's Chinese room name as a translation of the work.

facets.title: maker and attributed accounts
facets.question: Which voices are actually present, and which are missing?

reading.text: Available records support an affectionate and patriotic reading of Turner's relation to the picture, but that remains one maker's relation. A national icon is not a national voice, and an intended bequest does not establish one national view.

unknowns: No attributed account from crew members beyond named officers, the crews of Redoutable and Fougueux, builders, tow crews, breakers, forestry or fuel-supply workers, or nearby residents is present.
Institutional catalogue prose is not those people speaking.

facets.title: matter, ecology, energy, labour
facets.question: What material and work made the ship, tow, dismantling, and painting possible?

reading.text: Forest material, naval and river labour, wind, steam, salvage, reused canvas, paint chemistry, and conservation meet here. Reuse is visible at ship and canvas scale; ecological sustainability is not proven.

unknowns: The timber's forests of origin and regrowth are not established here.
The tug fuel, emissions, wider supply chains, and workers' names, pay, and health are not established here.
No lifecycle or carbon account exists in this record.

facets.title: exchange, ownership, power, displacement
facets.question: Who could command, sell, keep, and circulate the ship and image?

reading.text: The sequence runs from state weapon, to obsolete asset, to private raw material, to artist-held image, to public collection and currency symbol. Heroic commemoration can foreground victory while leaving harmed crews and labour outside the frame.

unknowns: The affected people's accounts and the full distribution of economic benefit are not present.
No source here establishes shared public choice or consensus around later national commemoration.

facets.title: knowledge and skill
facets.question: What does each kind of record know?

reading.text: The painting, eyewitness drawing, archive, and X-ray know different things. Their disagreement is the lesson: art can carry a true relation without becoming an eyewitness document.

unknowns: Tacit and first-person knowledge from builders, sailors, tow crews, and breakers is absent.

facets.title: continuity, rupture, repair
facets.question: What ended, what continued, and what was actually repaired?

reading.text: Dismantling is rupture; salvage is reuse; lining is conservation; bequest changes custody and access. No repair of harms from warfare or labour is evidenced here, and none of these acts supplies the missing accounts.

unknowns: No affected party has named a repair in this record.
Material continuity, image continuity, and institutional continuity must not be treated as interchangeable.

facets.title: present consequence
facets.question: What can be observed now, and what cannot be inferred from it?

reading.text: Free admission and appearance on currency are observed forms of access and circulation. They bind art, state memory, and exchange in daily life, but they do not prove shared understanding, wellbeing, sustainability, or thriving.

unknowns: Actual access and reception differ among people and are not measured here.
No causal effect on evidence, access, care, sustainability, or thriving is established.

uncertainties: Turner probably did not witness the tow and may not have been in England.
The actual hull was mastless, used two tugs, and arrived before sunset; Turner restored masts, made one tug dominant, and invented the sunset.
Turner's attitude to steam and industrial modernity is not reduced here to one position.
The current evidence base is institution-heavy and contains no environmental lifecycle account or authorised affected-party account.

quotes.text: …a noble river-piece by J.M.W. Turner, Esq., R.A., 'The Fighting Temeraire' — as grand a picture as ever figured on the walls of any academy, or came from the easel of any painter. The old Temeraire is dragged to her last home by a little, spiteful, diabolical steamer.

works.title: The Concert
works.one_line: three musicians nobody has heard since 1990 — the most valuable silence in the world
works.location_now: missing since 18 March 1990 — its frame waits, empty, in the Dutch Room of the Gardner Museum, Boston

feeling.text: Three people are making music you will never hear: a young woman at a harpsichord, a man with his back to us and a lute across his lap, a singer keeping time with one raised hand. The room is all held breath — Vermeer gives you the instant just before or just after sound. Behind them hangs a rowdy brothel scene, Baburen's Procuress, appetite and noise locked inside the stillness. One scholar calls the mood 'an impalpable air of reticence and introspection, unique among genre painters.' Since 18 March 1990 the picture holds a second silence: in the Gardner Museum's Dutch Room its gilded frame hangs empty on the wall, and people stand before the emptiness the way they once stood before the paint. The absence has become part of the work.

hands.text: Delft, around 1664. Vermeer is in his early thirties, living in his mother-in-law Maria Thins's house on the Oude Langendijk — the Catholic corner of a Protestant town, beside a hidden Jesuit church. His studio is the upstairs front room, lit from the north. The house is crowded: Catharina will bear fifteen children, and eleven are alive when he dies. He works with almost unreasonable slowness — perhaps three paintings a year — for a small circle of Delft buyers, above all Pieter van Ruijven and his wife Maria de Knuijt. At thirty he was elected a head of the painters' Guild of Saint Luke, and re-elected the next year. He even painted his own household into the picture: the Baburen brothel scene on the back wall most likely belonged to Maria Thins herself.

facts.claim: Vermeer lived in Maria Thins's house on the Oude Langendijk in Delft, almost next to a hidden Jesuit church, and stayed there for life.
His studio was the front room of the second floor, facing north.
Catharina Bolnes bore 15 children, four buried before baptism; 11 were living at Vermeer's death.
He probably produced about three paintings a year on order; his chief patrons were Pieter van Ruijven and Maria de Knuijt.
In 1662 Vermeer was elected head of Delft's Guild of Saint Luke and was re-elected in 1663, 1670 and 1671.
The Dirck van Baburen 'Procuress' shown on the back wall of The Concert most likely belonged to Vermeer's mother-in-law Maria Thins, who kept a discreet collection of Utrecht Caravaggists.

world.text: The Concert was painted at the high tide of the Dutch Golden Age. The Republic was the richest trading nation in Europe; ordinary households bought pictures, and Delft — a canal town of potteries and breweries — supported a whole guild of painters. It did not last. War with England came in 1665, and 1672 became the rampjaar, the disaster year: France under Louis XIV invaded together with England and the German bishoprics of Münster and Cologne. In The Hague a mob lynched the statesmen Johan and Cornelis de Witt. The economy broke and never fully recovered, and the art market went down with it — Vermeer, a dealer as well as a painter, was left holding stock nobody would buy. He could not sell 'any of his art,' his widow wrote, and three years after the crash he was dead.

facts.claim: In 1672 the Dutch Republic was attacked simultaneously by France under Louis XIV, England, and the bishoprics of Münster and Cologne.
On 20 August 1672 a mob killed Johan and Cornelis de Witt; the Dutch economy never fully recovered from the crisis.

The art market collapsed in 1672 and Vermeer — dealer as well as painter — was ruined, left holding stock nobody would buy. No formal bankruptcy occurred in his lifetime: the insolvency (cessio bonorum) was petitioned by his widow Catharina in April 1676, months after his death.
Vermeer inherited the family art-dealing business from his father and was left sitting with other masters' paintings he was dealing in when the war killed the market.
In July 1675, months before his death, Vermeer borrowed 1,000 guilders from an Amsterdam merchant.

paint.text: The Concert is oil on canvas, about 72.5 by 64.7 centimetres. Vermeer's great extravagance was blue: natural ultramarine, ground from lapis lazuli carried from Afghanistan, a pigment costlier than gold in the seventeenth century. Other painters saved it for a robe; Vermeer worked it into shadows, whitewashed walls, and gray mixtures of lead white, bone black and raw umber, so that his daylight glows in a way cheaper azurite never could. Around the blue sat a small, disciplined palette — lead-tin yellow for warm lights, madder lake for red glazes, green earth in shadowed flesh. The habit was ruinous arithmetic: exorbitant blue, perhaps three pictures a year, eleven children to feed. When he died in December 1675, aged 43, the baker held a bill of 617 guilders — roughly three years of bread — and his widow settled it with two paintings.

pigments.name: Natural ultramarine
pigments.note: Ground and washed from lapis lazuli imported from Afghanistan; more expensive than gold in the 17th century. Vermeer, unusually, laid it into shadows, jugs, walls and gray tones, not just blue things.

pigments.name: Lead white
pigments.note: The body of his daylight; mixed with bone black and raw umber into grays that Vermeer seeded with ultramarine for a luminosity 'which cannot be produced otherwise.'

pigments.name: Lead-tin yellow
pigments.note: His characteristic warm yellow for lit fabrics and highlights.

pigments.name: Madder lake
pigments.note: A transparent red glaze made from the root of the madder plant.

pigments.name: Green earth
pigments.note: A quiet Vermeer signature, used to cool and soften shadowed flesh tones.

pigments.name: Bone black and raw umber
pigments.note: The dark half of his gray mixtures, blended with lead white and a touch of ultramarine.

facts.claim: The Concert is dated c. 1664 and measures 72.5 x 64.7 cm.
Natural ultramarine was made from lapis lazuli imported from Afghanistan and was more expensive than gold in the 17th century.

No other 17th-century artist employed the exorbitantly expensive ultramarine so lavishly; only about 34 paintings are universally attributed to Vermeer today (a handful more are disputed, giving counts up to about 37).
Vermeer owed baker Hendrick van Buyten 617 guilders and 6 stuivers — about three years of bread — and in February 1676 his widow transferred two paintings to the baker against the debt.
Vermeer died in December 1675 aged 43 and was buried in Delft's Oude Kerk; sources disagree on the exact day (13-15 December).
Vermeer's widow Catharina petitioned for bankruptcy in April 1676; on 30 September 1676 the microscopist Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was appointed trustee of the estate.

afterlife.text: The painting's early history is murky; by the 1860s it belonged to Théophile Thoré-Bürger, the French critic who rescued Vermeer from oblivion. At his estate sale in Paris in 1892, Isabella Stewart Gardner had an agent bid for her, signalling with a wave of her handkerchief, and beat the Louvre — for about $5,000. It hung in her Boston museum until 1:24 a.m. on 18 March 1990, when two men in police uniforms and false moustaches talked their way in. 'Gentlemen, this is a robbery.' They duct-taped the two guards to a pipe and a workbench in the basement and spent 81 minutes taking thirteen works, worth some $500 million. The empty frames still hang in the Dutch Room. The reward stands at $10 million; the statute of limitations has expired; the FBI says it knows who the thieves were and that both are dead — it never released the names. The Concert, valued around $250 million, is widely called the most valuable stolen artwork still missing.

facts.claim: Isabella Stewart Gardner bought The Concert at the 1892 Paris auction of Théophile Thoré-Bürger's estate, bidding through an agent she signalled with her handkerchief, outbidding the Louvre and the National Gallery; accounts of the price vary between $5,000 and $6,000.
At 1:24 a.m. on 18 March 1990, two men in police uniforms claiming to respond to a disturbance were let in through the museum's employee entrance; the guards were restrained in the basement.
The thieves announced 'Gentlemen, this is a robbery,' duct-taped the guards to a pipe and workbench in the basement, and spent 81 minutes taking 13 works now valued at about $500 million.
The thieves, wearing false moustaches, spent one hour and twenty-one minutes in the galleries; the guards were bound with duct tape and taped to pipes in the basement.
Empty frames still hang in the Dutch Room gallery, both in homage to the missing works and as placeholders for their return.
In 2017 the museum doubled its reward from $5 million to $10 million, and its trustees later extended the $10 million offer indefinitely (plus $100,000 for the Napoleonic eagle finial).

The statute of limitations expired in 1995; no arrests, nothing recovered. The FBI said in 2013 it knew the thieves' identities and in 2015 that both were dead — it never released names. The names in circulation (Reissfelder, DiMuzio) come from Boston Globe reporting and a leaked internal FBI theory, and the identification remains disputed.

The Concert is thought to be the most valuable artwork currently unrecovered, with a value estimated at US$250 million — a figure traced to investigative reporters Stephen Kurkjian (Master Thieves, 2015) and Ulrich Boser (The Gardner Heist, 2009).
Artnet News likewise headlines The Concert as 'The World's Most Valuable Stolen Painting.'
The 1990 Gardner theft remains the largest art heist in modern history; the FBI's value estimate rose from $200 million in 1990 to $500 million.

quotes.text: During the ruinous war with France he not only was unable to sell any of his art but also, to his great detriment, was left sitting with the paintings of other masters that he was dealing in... owing to the great burden of his children, having no means of his own, he lapsed into such decay and decadence, which he had so taken to heart that, as if he had fallen into a frenzy, in a day and a half he went from being healthy to being dead.
quotes.who: Catharina Bolnes, Vermeer's widow, in her bankruptcy petition, 1676
One of the two thieves, to the Gardner Museum's night guards, 18 March 1990

quotes.text: One day, with enough careful observing, I knew I would solve the riddle of this painting. Now, I never will unless the painting is returned.
quotes.who: Lloyd Schwartz, poet and critic, on The Concert

works.title: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies — the First Folio
works.artist: William Shakespeare; gathered by John Heminges & Henry Condell, printed by William & Isaac Jaggard
works.one_line: two actors gathered their dead friend's plays so they would not vanish — half of Shakespeare survives only because they did
works.location_now: ≈235 copies survive of ~750 printed; 82 live at the Folger, Washington D.C. — all shown together since June 2024

feeling.text: It looks, at first, like any big old book: browned paper, heavy boards, a matter-of-fact title. Then the label tells you what you are standing over — the only door through which half of Shakespeare reached us — and the plainness turns to vertigo. Without this object there is no Macbeth, no Tempest, no Twelfth Night; words you have carried all your life nearly went nowhere. When the Folger sent Folios to all fifty states in 2016, each opened to 'To be or not to be', staff watched people stand over the page with tears running down their faces, and one visitor proposed marriage beside it. The feeling is not really about rarity or price. It is gratitude with a shiver in it: the sudden arithmetic of how close it all came to never.

hands.text: Shakespeare died in 1616 with no collected edition; about half his plays had never been printed at all. Two actors fixed that: John Heminges and Henry Condell, his friends and fellow shareholders in the King's Men, who gathered scripts, playhouse copies, and earlier quartos into one book, 'onely to keepe the memory of so worthy a Friend, & Fellow aliue.' The printing, from early 1622 to late 1623, happened in the shop of William Jaggard — old, blind, and dying; he was gone about a month before the book went on sale, so his son Isaac carried it through. At least five compositors set the type, each betrayed by his own spelling habits. The clumsiest, 'Compositor E', was almost certainly John Leason, a teenager apprenticed only in November 1622, whose mistakes still speckle the pages he set. Eighteen plays — Macbeth, The Tempest, Twelfth Night among them — exist because of these hands.

facts.claim: Heminges and Condell, Shakespeare's friends and fellow King's Men, assembled 36 plays seven years after his death in 1616; 18 of them — including Macbeth, The Tempest, Twelfth Night, Julius Caesar, As You Like It and The Winter's Tale — had never been printed and would likely be lost otherwise.

Printing ran from about February 1622 to early November 1623 at the Jaggard shop; William Jaggard was old, infirm and blind by 1623 and died about a month before the book went on sale, so most of the work fell to his son Isaac.

Five compositors (A–E), identified by their spelling and typesetting habits, set the book: A set 194 pages, B 445, C 120, D 35½, E 71½. Compositor E was most likely John Leason, whose apprenticeship contract dated only from 4 November 1622.
John Leason 'started as a teenage apprentice at the Jaggards' in November 1622'; 'his lack of experience meant he made many mistakes,' and errors survive throughout the Folio.

In the preface 'To the great Variety of Readers', Heminges and Condell say they 'collected & publish'd' the plays where readers had been 'abus'd with diuerse stolne, and surreptitious copies, maimed, and deformed'.

world.text: London in 1623 was a city that had learned to live with plague: the outbreaks of 1603 and 1608–09 killed tens of thousands and shut the playhouses for months at a stretch — closures the King's Men knew in their wages. The book trade crowded into St Paul's Churchyard, in the shadow of the cathedral, and when the Folio finally went on sale in late 1623 Edward Blount took delivery at his shop there, at the sign of the Black Bear. It was a luxury object: 15 shillings unbound, about £1 bound in plain calf — while a good set of knives cost 12 shillings and Ben Jonson's own folio Workes just 9. Sir Edward Dering bought two copies at £1 each; for an ordinary worker, one scholar reckons, that £1 felt like spending thousands of dollars today. Roughly 750 copies were printed.

facts.claim: An unbound First Folio cost 15 shillings in 1623; a copy in plain calf binding cost £1 (20 shillings). About 750 copies were printed.
Edward Blount, principal publisher with the Jaggards, sold the Folio from his bookshop at the sign of the Black Bear in St Paul's Churchyard from late 1623.

Sir Edward Dering bought two First Folios in 1623 for £1 each; 'to the average worker, spending £1 on a book in 1623 would probably have seemed like spending around $4,000 or more for one today' — a set of knives cost 12 shillings, Ben Jonson's folio 9 shillings.

The 1603 plague killed around a quarter of London's population and kept the theatres closed for nearly a year; severe outbreaks recurred in 1592–93, 1603–04, 1606 and 1608–09, repeatedly costing Shakespeare's company its playhouse income.
Plague closures shaped Shakespeare's working life and writing; the Folger documents the closures and their traces in the plays.

paint.text: England in 1623 had no mill making paper fine enough to print on, so the Folio's sheets — almost 230 per copy — came from northern France: white paper of pounded linen rags, folded and nested three sheets at a time into gatherings of six leaves. The paper alone cost the publishers as much as all the setting and printing. The text runs in two columns, roman type for the spoken lines, italic for names and stage directions — around four million pieces of type lifted letter by letter for some 900 pages. On the title page sits Martin Droeshout's copper engraving, cut by a man in his early twenties who probably never saw Shakespeare alive. The plate exists in four states; in the rare first state the head floats eerily above the collar, missing its shadow — only four such impressions survive. Facing it, Ben Jonson supplies the correction: since the engraver could not draw the wit, 'looke / Not on his Picture, but his Booke.'

pigments.name: French linen rag paper
pigments.note: No English mill then produced printing-quality paper, so it was imported from northern France, made from the fibres of linen rags; the paper cost as much as the typesetting and printing combined.

pigments.name: Folio sheets, folded in sixes
pigments.note: Almost 230 sheets per copy, each printed both sides and folded once; three sheets nested made a gathering of six leaves (twelve pages) — a 'folio in sixes'.

pigments.name: Roman and italic type
pigments.note: Dialogue set in roman, stage directions and speech headings in italic, two columns per page; about four million pieces of type were set for the Folio's 908 pages.

pigments.name: Copper-plate engraving (Droeshout portrait)
pigments.note: Martin Droeshout's engraving exists in four states; state 1 lacks the shadow behind the head so it seems to float above the collar — only four impressions survive (two at the Folger, one British Library, one Bodleian).

facts.claim: Dialogue appears in roman type with stage directions and speech prefixes in italic, in a two-column layout, as the Bodleian's digital First Folio transcription records.
Martin Droeshout the Younger was born in 1601 — about 22 when the Folio appeared — and very likely never met Shakespeare; the portrait was probably worked from an existing likeness.
Ben Jonson's verse 'To the Reader' faces the portrait and ends: 'Reader, looke / Not on his Picture, but his Booke.'
The Droeshout portrait is one of very few images of Shakespeare considered authentic.

afterlife.text: Of roughly 750 copies, 235 are known today, each tracked like a person with a biography. The Folger Shakespeare Library in Washington holds 82; Meisei University in Tokyo holds 12. In October 2020 the copy Mills College had owned since 1977 sold at Christie's New York for $9,978,000 — a record at auction for any work of literature. New ones still surface: in 2016 a three-volume copy annotated by the eighteenth-century editor Isaac Reed was authenticated at Mount Stuart, on the Isle of Bute. And they are stolen. Durham University's Folio vanished in 1998; a decade on, Raymond Scott walked it into the Folger stripped of its binding and title leaf, spinning a tale of friends in Cuba — eight years for handling stolen goods, and death in his cell in 2012. In 1940 a gang lifted Williams College's copy behind a fake professor's card; it came home within the year. Manchester's, taken in 1972, is missing still.

facts.claim: About 750 copies were printed; 235 are known to survive, and the Folger Shakespeare Library holds 82 of them — the world's largest collection.
Meisei University in Tokyo holds 12 First Folios, the largest collection outside the Folger.

On 14 October 2020 the Mills College copy sold at Christie's New York for $9,978,000 to book dealer Stephan Loewentheil — a world auction record for a work of literature, against an estimate of $4–6 million.

In April 2016 a First Folio was authenticated by Oxford professor Emma Smith at Mount Stuart on the Isle of Bute — an unusual three-volume copy once owned and annotated by the 18th-century editor Isaac Reed.

Durham University's First Folio was stolen in December 1998; in 2008 Raymond Scott brought it to the Folger for authentication, its binding, title page and end leaves cut away; in 2010 he was convicted of handling stolen goods and jailed for eight years, and in 2012 he was found dead in his cell at HMP Northumberland.

On 8 February 1940 the Kwiatkowski gang stole Williams College's First Folio from the Chapin Library, using an accomplice posing as 'Professor Sinclair E. Gillingham' of Middlebury; the book was recovered undamaged and returned on 21 October 1940, and all four men were convicted.
The First Folio stolen from the John Rylands Library, Manchester, on 13 July 1972 has never been recovered.

During the Folger's 2016 tour of Folios to all 50 states, each copy displayed open to 'To be or not to be', visitors stood over the book with tears running down their faces, and one person proposed marriage in front of it.

quotes.text: We haue but collected them, and done an office to the dead … onely to keepe the memory of so worthy a Friend, & Fellow aliue, as was our Shakespeare.
quotes.where: 'To the great Variety of Readers', the First Folio's preface, 1623

quotes.text: He was not of an age, but for all time!
quotes.where: 'To the memory of my beloued, The Avthor Mr. William Shakespeare', prefatory poem in the First Folio, 1623
